comments.author: Ada N
comments.body: Design wants the minus before the dollar sign for refunds, same as on the receipts.

content.summary: Format amounts as dollars with separators, including refunds.
content.task: Write `formatPrice(cents)`: return the amount in dollars with two decimals and comma thousands separators, e.g. `123456` → `"$1,234.56"`. Negative amounts are refunds and get a leading minus: `-500` → `"-$5.00"`.
content.title: Cart shows prices as raw cents

comments.author: Jo T
comments.body: 40 tickets this morning. People type codes the way they read them in the email.

comments.author: Lena M
comments.body: Black Friday is in two weeks, so this one jumps the queue.

content.summary: Match promo codes case-insensitively and ignore stray spaces.
content.task: `applyDiscount(totalCents, code, codes)` returns the total after the matching code's percentage off, rounded down to whole cents. Codes match case-insensitively and ignoring surrounding spaces; an unknown code leaves the total unchanged.
content.title: Discount codes fail when typed in lowercase

comments.author: Ada N
comments.body: The accessibility audit flagged every checkbox here. Clicking the text should toggle the box.

expected: <form><label for="filter-in-stock">in-stock</label><input type="checkbox" id="filter-in-stock" name="in-stock"><label for="filter-on-sale">on-sale</label><input type="checkbox" id="filter-on-sale" name="on-sale"></form>
content.summary: Tie every filter checkbox to a label so it is accessible.
content.task: Render the product filter form: for each filter name, a `<label for="filter-NAME">` with the name as text, followed by `<input type="checkbox" id="filter-NAME" name="NAME">`, all inside a `<form>`.
content.title: Product filter checkboxes have no labels

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: Search API gets about eight requests per query. 300 ms after the last keystroke is plenty.

hints: Each keystroke cancels the pending request if it arrives before the timer fires.
content.summary: Debounce search-as-you-type so the API sees one request per pause.
content.task: `debounceTimes(keystrokes, waitMs)`: given keystroke times in milliseconds, return the times at which the debounced search fires. It fires `waitMs` after a keystroke unless another keystroke comes first.
content.title: Search box sends a request on every keystroke

comments.author: Mateo O
comments.body: The mobile app sends per_page=500 to fetch everything in one go. Cap it, don't error.

content.summary: Parse page and per_page with defaults and a hard cap.
content.task: `ParsePage(query)` reads `page` and `per_page` from a URL query string. Defaults are page 1 and 20 per page, `per_page` is capped at 100, and missing, zero, negative or non-numeric values fall back to the default.
content.title: List endpoints accept any page size

comments.author: Jo T
comments.body: Customers say reset emails 'never work'. They do, if you click within a minute.

content.summary: The TTL is in minutes but the check compares seconds.
content.task: `isExpired(issuedAt, now, ttlMinutes)` with Unix timestamps in seconds. A link issued at t stays valid until `t + ttlMinutes × 60`, inclusive.
content.title: Password reset links expire after a minute

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: Credential-stuffing bot again last night. A sliding window per IP, nothing fancy.

hints: Keep only the timestamps still inside the window.
content.summary: Allow at most n attempts in any sliding window.
content.task: Write `allow(times, limit, windowMs)`: for each login attempt time, return whether it is allowed when at most `limit` attempts may fall inside any window of `windowMs` milliseconds.
content.title: Rate-limit login attempts

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: Alerting is blind to the 502s because duration and status come back empty.

comments.author: Priya K
comments.body: Durations are always whole milliseconds, suffixed with ms.

content.summary: Turn an access log line into a structured record.
content.task: Write `ParseLine(line)` for lines like `GET /cart 200 12ms`, returning method, path, status and duration in milliseconds.
content.title: Access log parser drops fields on 5xx lines

comments.author: Priya K
comments.body: Every customer with a comma in their company name lands in the wrong column. 'Acme, Inc.' is our biggest account.

content.summary: Respect quoted fields when parsing partner exports.
content.task: `parse_csv_line(line)` splits a CSV line on commas, except inside double quotes. Quotes are removed, and a doubled quote inside a quoted field is a literal quote: `"say ""hi"""` → `say "hi"`.
content.title: CSV import splits company names on commas

comments.author: Lena M
comments.body: Marketing sent last week's newsletter three times to some people. They were not thrilled.

content.summary: Keep the first record per email before the newsletter sync.
content.task: `dedupe(records)` keeps the first record for each email, comparing emails case-insensitively and ignoring surrounding spaces. Keep the original order.
content.title: Deduplicate customer records by email

comments.author: Rui F
comments.body: Just the totals per customer, biggest first. The chart is my job.

content.summary: Total each customer's orders, biggest first.
content.task: Given `orders(id, customer, total)`, select each customer and the sum of their totals, highest first.
content.title: Revenue by customer for the monthly report

comments.author: Rui F
comments.body: Month-end close is Friday. I need this list before then.

hints: A LEFT JOIN keeps orders even when no payment matches.
content.summary: Reconcile orders against payments before month-end close.
content.task: Given `orders(id, customer)` and `payments(order_id, amount)`, select the ids of orders that have no payment, smallest first.
content.title: Find orders with no matching payment

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: No malloc on the hot path. Fixed-size array, overwrite the oldest.

content.summary: A fixed-size buffer that overwrites its oldest entry.
content.task: Implement a ring buffer of capacity `n`. Given a sequence of pushes, return the contents oldest first.
content.title: Keep the last N request latencies in memory

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: The current version re-sorts every sample for every percentile. Busy hours have two million samples.

content.summary: Compute nearest-rank percentiles for the metrics endpoint.
content.task: `percentile(samples, p)` returns the nearest-rank percentile: sort the samples and take the value at rank `ceil(p / 100 × n)`, counting from 1. Return `null` when there are no samples.
content.title: p99 latency panel times out in busy hours

comments.author: Mateo O
comments.body: Hit rate dropped to 12% after the last deploy. I think get() stopped refreshing recency.

hints: Pair a hash map with a doubly linked list ordered by last use.
content.summary: Reads must refresh recency in the LRU cache.
content.task: Simulate an LRU cache with the given capacity over operations `["put", key, value]` and `["get", key]`. Return the results of the gets in order, `-1` for a miss. A get counts as a use.
content.title: Cache evicts entries that were just used

comments.author: Sam R
comments.body: Somebody set idle_timeout = 3600 meaning minutes. Let people write 1h.

content.summary: Accept durations like 1h30m in config files.
content.task: `parse_duration(text)` turns strings like `"1h30m"`, `"45s"` or `"2h"` into seconds. Units are `h`, `m` and `s`, each at most once and in that order; return `null` for anything else.
content.title: Timeouts in config must be written in seconds

content.story:
The online shop customers actually see: product listings, filters, the cart and a three-step checkout. Pages are server-rendered, with a thin layer of TypeScript for the interactive parts.

Conversion dipped after the last redesign. Support is fielding tickets about prices, promo codes and a search box that feels sluggish, and an accessibility audit came back with a long list.

## What you'll work on

- Formatting money and other values the way customers expect to read them
- Form behaviour, validation and accessible markup
- Small performance fixes in the browser, like debouncing input

## Good fit if you

- Build user interfaces, or want to get sharper at the details that make one feel solid
- Are comfortable with **JavaScript**, **TypeScript** or plain **HTML**
- Care what a bug looks like from the customer's side of the screen

Stack: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML.
content.summary: Frontend: the customer-facing shop, cart and checkout.
content.title: Storefront

content.story:
The service every client talks to for sign-up, login, sessions and password resets. Most of it is Go, a few older endpoints are still PHP, and the login gateway in front is TypeScript.

It mostly works, and the on-call channel has opinions about the rest: list endpoints that accept any page size, reset links that expire too soon, and logs that are hard to search during an incident.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing and validating request parameters with sensible defaults
- Time and expiry logic, where off-by-one and unit mix-ups hide
- Rate limiting and log handling for the people on call

## Good fit if you

- Write backend services, or want practice with the bugs they actually get
- Like **input validation**, edge cases and reading a stack trace at 2am
- Know **Go**, **PHP** or **TypeScript**, or want to try one of them on familiar problems

Stack: Go, PHP, TypeScript.
content.summary: Backend: sign-up, login and account endpoints behind every app.
content.title: Accounts API

content.story:
Partners drop CSV exports in a bucket every night. A pipeline cleans them, loads the warehouse and feeds the reports finance reads on Monday morning.

The exports are messier than anyone admits: quoted commas in company names, duplicate customers with slightly different emails, and orders that never got paid. When the numbers look wrong, this is where people come asking.

## What you'll work on

- Parsing awkward input files without losing data
- Cleaning and deduplicating records before they reach the warehouse
- SQL for the reports and reconciliations people rely on

## Good fit if you

- Work with data, or are the person on your team who ends up writing the SQL
- Enjoy turning messy input into something you can trust
- Know **Python** and **SQL**, or want more practice with both

Stack: Python, SQL.
content.summary: Data: nightly partner imports, cleaning and the reports finance relies on.
content.title: Data platform

content.story:
A small proxy in front of everything: it terminates connections, caches hot responses and exports latency metrics. It's written in C, C++ and Rust, depending on who wrote which part and when.

Every allocation shows up on a flame graph here. The backlog is about doing more with fixed memory, measuring the right thing, and keeping configuration readable for whoever is paged.

## What you'll work on

- Fixed-size data structures such as ring buffers and LRU caches
- Latency percentiles and the metrics behind dashboards
- Small, strict configuration formats

## Good fit if you

- Do systems or performance work, or want to get closer to the metal
- Think about memory, ordering and what happens under load
- Know **C**, **C++** or **Rust**, or are learning one of them

Stack: C, C++, Rust.
content.summary: Systems: the low-latency proxy in front of everything.
content.title: Edge proxy
